q: You need help, but nobody aboard is in danger yet. Which call do you make on channel 16?
a: PAN-PAN
o: MAYDAY
SÉCURITÉ
MAYDAY RELAY
why: Urgent help needed but no grave and imminent danger: PAN-PAN.

q: You are about to send an urgency call to every station in range from your yacht Nefeli. How does it begin?
a: PAN-PAN ×3, ALL STATIONS ×3, THIS IS, Nefeli ×3
o: ALL STATIONS ×3, PAN-PAN ×3, THIS IS, Nefeli ×3
PAN-PAN once, ALL STATIONS once, THIS IS, Nefeli once
PAN-PAN ×3, THIS IS, Nefeli ×3, ALL STATIONS ×3
why: Urgency call: PAN-PAN three times, the station(s) called, THIS IS, your name three times.

q: Your crew member needs a doctor's view on what to do next. Which call do you make?
a: PAN-PAN, asking for medical advice
o: MAYDAY, asking for a helicopter
SÉCURITÉ, warning other yachts
A routine call to the Kos marina
why: Medical help needed but no immediate threat to life: PAN-PAN with medical advice requested.

q: You want a tow and only Olympia Radio needs to hear it. How do you address your PAN-PAN?
a: PAN-PAN ×3, then Olympia Radio ×3
o: PAN-PAN ×3, then ALL STATIONS ×3 only
Olympia Radio by voice on channel 70
PAN-PAN ×3 with no address at all
why: An urgency call may go to all stations or to one named station, three times after PAN-PAN.

q: Your problem has gone away on its own. What do you do about your earlier call?
a: Cancel the PAN-PAN: tell all stations you need no help
o: Nothing — an urgency call expires by itself
Send SEELONCE FEENEE on channel 16
Send a SÉCURITÉ that your engine runs
why: Cancel an urgency call once the urgency is over, so nobody keeps looking for you.

q: You pass this hazard in a busy channel. Which call warns the other vessels about it?
a: SÉCURITÉ
o: PAN-PAN
MAYDAY
MAYDAY RELAY
why: A danger to navigation is a safety message: SÉCURITÉ.

q: You hear a coast station on 16 begin: "SÉCURITÉ, SÉCURITÉ, SÉCURITÉ, all stations…". What kind of message follows?
a: A navigational or weather warning
o: A call for help from a vessel in danger
A distress call — 16 goes silent
A list of calls waiting for ships
why: SÉCURITÉ introduces a safety message: a navigational or weather warning.

q: A coast station announces a SÉCURITÉ on 16 and says the gale warning follows on another channel, which it names. What do you do?
a: Switch to the channel it named and listen
o: Reply on 16 to acknowledge the warning
Stay on 16 — the warning comes there
Ignore it unless your boat is named
why: The SÉCURITÉ is only announced on 16; the message itself goes out on the working channel given.

q: You have finished the opening of your PAN-PAN to all stations. What comes next?
a: Your position, the problem and help needed
o: Only your MMSI, then wait to be called
The word MAYDAY, then your position
Nothing — wait for the coastguard to ask
why: After the opening comes the message: position, nature of the urgency, assistance wanted.

q: Things have changed since your urgency call went out. What do you do on the radio now?
a: Upgrade to MAYDAY — the danger is now grave
o: Repeat the PAN-PAN every 15 minutes
Cancel the PAN-PAN and call a marina
Send a SÉCURITÉ warning of the rocks
why: When the danger becomes grave and imminent, the urgency call is upgraded to MAYDAY.

fig.title: Still drifting
lines: You sent PAN-PAN for a tow

q: You have announced a SÉCURITÉ on 16 about a drifting container. Where do you give the warning itself?
a: On a working channel you named on 16
o: On 16, straight after the announcement
On channel 70, as a DSC text message
Only to the coastguard, by phone
why: Keep 16 clear: announce there, then give the safety message on a working channel.

q: The coast station acknowledges your medical PAN-PAN on 16 and asks you to change to a working channel. What do you do?
a: Change channel and continue the talk there
o: Stay on 16 — urgency talk must stay there
Refuse — medical calls need channel 16
Cancel the PAN-PAN before you change
why: Long urgency traffic moves off 16 when the coast station asks, keeping 16 free.

q: Which of these situations calls for a PAN-PAN?
a: Engine dead, drifting offshore, no danger yet
o: Fire in the cabin that you cannot put out
A big log floating in the harbour approach
Booking a berth at the marina for tonight
why: PAN-PAN: urgent, but no grave and imminent danger. The fire is MAYDAY, the log SÉCURITÉ.

q: You need a tow to the nearest port. Which call fits, and why?
a: PAN-PAN — urgent, but no grave and imminent danger
o: MAYDAY — a dismasting is always a distress
SÉCURITÉ — warn others of the lost rig
No call — hail a passing yacht instead
why: Help is needed urgently, but boat and crew are not in grave and imminent danger: PAN-PAN.

fig.title: Dismasted
lines: Mast down, rig cut free and sunk

q: Your guest is getting worse by the minute. Which call do you make?
a: MAYDAY — a life is in grave and imminent danger
o: PAN-PAN — medical cases are always urgency
PAN-PAN, asking for medical advice only
SÉCURITÉ, asking any doctor to call you
why: A life-threatening condition is grave and imminent danger to a person: MAYDAY.

q: A coast station is reading a SÉCURITÉ announcement on 16 just as you want to call a friend's yacht. What do you do?
a: Wait until it ends, then make your call
o: Stay off 16 until SEELONCE FEENEE
Call over it — safety is low priority
Wait an hour before any routine call
why: Safety traffic comes before routine calls but imposes no silence: wait until it is over.

q: The coast station answers your medical PAN-PAN and puts you through to a doctor. Which information helps the doctor most?
a: Age, symptoms and the first aid given
o: Passport number and nationality
The name of their doctor at home
The boat's insurance details
why: Medical advice by radio needs the patient's age, symptoms and the treatment given so far.

q: You see that a big mooring buoy has broken free and is drifting into the harbour approach. May your yacht send a SÉCURITÉ?
a: Yes — any station may warn of a danger
o: No — only coast stations send SÉCURITÉ
Only with the coastguard's permission
Only by DSC, never by voice
why: Any station may send a safety message about a danger to navigation.

q: Halfway through your own message, someone else breaks in on channel 16. What do you do?
a: Stop, listen, and finish later if 16 is clear
o: Finish your SÉCURITÉ — you started first
Switch to high power and talk over it
Answer the PAN-PAN with your position
why: Urgency outranks safety: give way to the PAN-PAN, note it, and resume afterwards.

q: The coast station has your PAN-PAN; a lifeboat will reach you in an hour. How do you use the radio while you wait?
a: Keep a listening watch on 16 and as told
o: Switch off to save the battery till it comes
Call every five minutes for an update
Switch to 70 and wait for a DSC call
why: Stay reachable: keep watch on 16 or on the channel the coast station gave you.
